title: Transforming Law with AI: Generative Models, Innovation in Dispute Resolution, and Leadership in Change — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s view that AI can augment strategic work and still requires human expertise, but it does not address the principal succession, apprenticeship, leverage or career-pipeline proposition. Its anecdotes about ideation and business planning therefore neither establish nor reject that automated work weakens expertise-development routes.

It's another example of how these tools can be strategic in ways our human brains might take longer to reach.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s cautious, bounded approach and adds a concrete AAA implementation: a launched clause-drafting tool designed around nonlawyer needs and curated institutional expertise. It also reinforces the cluster’s distinction between fabricated authorities and ordinary interpretive mistakes, while offering implementation experience rather than measured evidence of accuracy or justice outcomes.
qs: Because, like I said earlier, not just individuals—but many businesses—have non-lawyers trying to make sure their contracts will serve them in the future if there’s a dispute.

But it occurred to us pretty early in our exploration of generative AI that we could use a library of perfected clauses—which we have, because we review clauses all the time for businesses who want to make sure they comply with our due process protocols, if they want us to adjudicate their cases someday.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s implementation thesis with a concrete AAA case: existing innovation infrastructure, broad-based experimentation, leadership and sustained change management enabled adoption, while limited staff time and short-term revenue incentives constrained it. It adds practical experience but no quantified evidence on productivity, pricing or staffing effects.
qs: And yet, I mean—it still requires enormous leadership and enormous change management to shift the goalposts.
If they take their foot off the billable hour gas, they’re letting go of revenue in the short term to try to figure this out.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source accepts that AI uptake is not itself service transformation and materially extends the cluster by identifying organizational innovation capacity, leadership and change management as prerequisites for effective deployment. It offers organizational experience rather than evidence of sustained access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: But the structured, robust innovation practice was already there—I didn’t have to build it.
And yet, I mean—it still requires enormous leadership and enormous change management to shift the goalposts.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source accepts practitioner-led experimentation despite uncertainty and materially extends the cluster with AAA’s concrete organizational implementation: a beta-tested, fine-tuned Clause Builder AI built from internal expertise. It also recognizes hallucinations and other risks as legitimate barriers rather than reasons for blanket disengagement.
qs: So we wanted to share what we've learned along the way—resources, our experiences working with generative AI, and an optimistic perspective about how this technology can transform legal services, legal education, and the practice of law for the better.
The Clause Builder AI tool—which went live a few weeks ago (we had it in beta for a while as we fine-tuned it)—is a version of our legacy Clause Builder tool.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts legal AI as organisational and service redesign and materially extends the proposition with AAA’s concrete implementation model: organisation-wide participation, customer discovery, an innovation pipeline, staff incentives and protected capacity. It also reinforces that leadership and change management—not tool acquisition alone—determine adoption, while acknowledging unresolved workload constraints and unmeasured outcomes.
qs: We move those ideas to Go Teams for design sprints, gather user data and input—customer discovery—and then move things quickly through an innovation pipeline into practice.
If we’re asking people to do this, we have to make sure they have the room to do it.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, human-centred deployment and materially extends the cluster’s operating-model argument with a concrete organisation-wide R&D approach: staff with operational knowledge identify use cases, supported experimentation builds internal capability, and AI handles suitable task components while humans focus on user-critical work. Its dispute-resolution and access-to-justice claims are prospective rather than established, consistent with the cluster’s caution about realised outcomes.
qs: He’s figuring out what are the ways this technology can really impact our jobs in a positive way—how we can move parts of the job that AI can do easily to the technology, and focus our human attention on the parts that make a difference for the users who depend on us.
There’s no way this can be a tech-only solution.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on expert-guided AI use and organisational investment in learning: it argues that effective use requires enough expertise to assess suggestions and that billable-hour incentives constrain experimentation. It does not directly establish the cluster’s central causal claim that automation is removing the junior work through which expertise is developed.
qs: Again, we'll talk more about this with your experience, but I think these tools work best when you come in with creative ideas and also enough expertise to know which suggestions are going to work and which aren't.
If they take their foot off the billable hour gas, they’re letting go of revenue in the short term to try to figure this out.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s practical, organisation-guided approach to continuous AI adaptation. It argues that employee use is already occurring despite gaps in strategy and training, so organisations should shape experimentation rather than wait, ban use or leave it unmanaged. Its survey evidence is explicitly caveated and concerns knowledge workers generally, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary limits.
qs: And, you know, take it for what it is—Microsoft obviously has a vested interest in the Gen AI world—but it shows that over 70% of knowledge workers are actively using AI, whether your organization has an AI strategy or not.
So you have an opportunity to shape how they use it—or they’re just going to go rogue and use it however they think is most helpful.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The source supports AI-enabled process redesign to expand affordable dispute resolution beyond conventional arbitration, mediation and litigation, especially for unmet civil legal need. It presents human involvement as context-dependent rather than endorsing universal machine adjudication, while its claimed access, speed, fairness and trust benefits remain prospective rather than demonstrated.
qs: As Colin Rule, the CEO of ODR.com, says: “We want to fit the forum to the fuss.” And sometimes, an ODR product—an online dispute resolution product, maybe with a mediator and maybe without—could be a better forum for a particular fuss.

I think this new technology—and a mission-driven entrepreneur like Colin Rule, who genuinely wants to change the way humanity resolves disputes—gives us an opportunity to reach this big blue ocean that lawyers couldn’t fish in before.I think there will now be tools that provide an operating system for people to resolve disputes—and for lawyers, frankly, to help them.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core conclusion that Claude can produce useful, faster legal-facing work without demonstrating autonomous practice. Its examples remain anecdotal and explicitly depend on human expertise to select, adapt and validate uneven AI suggestions; it does not materially address whether general platforms will displace specialist legal software.
qs: Again, we'll talk more about this with your experience, but I think these tools work best when you come in with creative ideas and also enough expertise to know which suggestions are going to work and which aren't.
We found ways to adapt those ideas for a legal audience, and it saved us a ton of time while really benefiting our clients.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core reliability proposition by describing generative outputs as probabilistic rather than reasoned, acknowledging unstable answers, and illustrating realised legal harm through a fabricated case citation filed in federal court. It does not materially address mitigation efficacy, verification costs or broader empirical error rates.
qs: But that’s my understanding of hallucinations—it’s that sort of probabilistic outcome that is non-existent in our sense of reality.

And of course, the most famous example that set us all back months in the conversation is the ChatGPT lawyer from last year, where ChatGPT hallucinated a case name that didn’t exist, and the lawyer filed a brief containing that case name with a federal court.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI value depends on organisational absorption rather than access alone. It identifies supported experimentation and internal capability-building as practical adoption mechanisms, while showing how workload, billable-hour incentives and hallucination cases constrain learning and uptake. It does not establish broader productivity or business-model effects.
qs: There was no, “Here’s how you learn to code with these tools.” But our engineers did the same thing—we brought in some help, but we made sure everybody had the information they needed to start experimenting.
If they take their foot off the billable hour gas, they’re letting go of revenue in the short term to try to figure this out.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source endorses sustained learning and an optimistic but risk-aware approach to generative AI, while arguing that organisations should act now by establishing guidance and strategy because employees are already using the technology. Its adoption claims are partly predictive or weakly evidenced, but that limitation is consistent with the cluster’s characterization of the case as an agenda for action rather than demonstrated outcomes.

And if you want to make sure they’re using it in ways you think are appropriate, it might make sense to figure out a strategy for your organization—and also think about the cost of not putting a strategy together.”  And I think people are convinced by that in a way they may not yet be convinced by some of the upside.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports selective augmentation: generative AI can save time and broaden creative or strategic options, but useful outputs depend on human expertise to filter and adapt suggestions. It also reinforces concern about hallucinations and contextual error, while offering anecdotes rather than measured evidence and not addressing junior development or staffing leverage.
qs: Again, we'll talk more about this with your experience, but I think these tools work best when you come in with creative ideas and also enough expertise to know which suggestions are going to work and which aren't.

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account that hallucinations remain a significant trust and adoption barrier. It specifically reinforces the distinction between fabricated authorities and the interpretive or contextual mistakes made by inexperienced lawyers, while offering anecdotal rather than measured evidence about adoption impact or verification cost.
qs: Bridget McCormack: Yeah, and it’s definitely been a significant stumbling block for a lot of uptake in legal—and understandably so.

You might have a junior lawyer who doesn’t understand the holding of a case or misses a nuance, but they’re generally not submitting work product to a judge or a partner that has completely made-up case names.

kp.k: AAA's scale provides substantial operational scope for AI
kp.d: McCormack describes AAA as a global arbitration and mediation provider with private dispute-resolution data. She reports over half a million cases administered last year, 28 US offices and one in Singapore, about 720 AAA–ICDR employees, and over 5,000 independent-contractor panelists. These are organizational self-reports, not measured AI outcomes; she distinguishes AAA's contract disputes from state courts' mixed civil and criminal caseloads.
qs: Last year, we administered over half a million cases, just to give you a sense of the volume.
There are about 720 people who work for the AAA–ICDR right now.
The AAA has over 5,000 panelists—independent contractors, not employees, but important members of our community.

kp.k: Existing innovation infrastructure accelerated AAA's AI transition
kp.d: McCormack says anticipated rapid changes to legal practice and business prompted leadership education and organization-wide exploration when she started in February 2023. An existing innovation vice president, team, BrightIdea platform, design sprints and customer-discovery pipeline enabled the transition. All employees received three hours of innovation training within her first two months; she presents establishing such infrastructure as the first step for organizations lacking it.
qs: I didn’t start the job until February 2023.
every single person across the organization did three hours of innovation training.
We move those ideas to Go Teams for design sprints, gather user data and input—customer discovery—and then move things quickly through an innovation pipeline into practice.

kp.k: Employee-led task mapping explores potential job redesign
kp.d: McCormack reports that marketing employee Jason Cabrera used HR job tasks to ask several LLMs which tasks they could handle at least 50% of without additional tools, then repeated the exercise with tools or context. His resulting matrix and proposed internal academy illustrate exploratory workforce planning based on model self-assessments, rather than demonstrated task automation or measured productivity gains.
qs: asked each LLM to evaluate which tasks it could handle 50% or more of with no additional tools.
Then he asked a second set of questions, this time giving the models various additional tools or context, and had each model create a matrix for him.
Now he's proposing we set up an internal academy so all of our staff can start thinking now about how their jobs might change and how they can take advantage of those changes for the better.

kp.k: Generative AI supports expert-guided creative and strategic work
kp.d: Leonard recounts using Claude 3.5 Sonnet to design lawyer workshops and another LLM to reconsider business revenue streams, including prioritizing sustainable projects over larger one-off engagements. She reports time savings and novel ideas but emphasizes expertise in rejecting unsuitable suggestions and adapting useful ones. These are personal experiences, not quantified evaluations.
qs: I think these tools work best when you come in with creative ideas and also enough expertise to know which suggestions are going to work and which aren't.
We found ways to adapt those ideas for a legal audience, and it saved us a ton of time while really benefiting our clients.
The LLM actually suggested prioritizing more sustainable projects—even if they're lower in dollar value—when it came to long-term strategy.

kp.k: Probabilistic outputs complicate lawyers' expectations of technological reliability
kp.d: McCormack contrasts variable probabilistic outputs with fixed, reproducible deterministic outputs, arguing that lawyers' familiarity with the latter contributes to discomfort with LLMs. She also compares nuanced disagreement between lawyers to probabilistic variation. Leonard distinguishes ordinary junior-lawyer mistakes from fabricated case names and recalls a lawyer filing a nonexistent ChatGPT-generated case; both speakers identify hallucination publicity as an adoption barrier, without reporting error rates.
qs: A probabilistic AI model generates outputs based on probability distributions.
Deterministic is when outputs are fixed for a given input.

You might have a junior lawyer who doesn’t understand the holding of a case or misses a nuance, but they’re generally not submitting work product to a judge or a partner that has completely made-up case names.

kp.k: Distributed experimentation includes staff, panelists and engineers
kp.d: McCormack describes voluntary staff user groups receiving $20/month GPT licenses and later Claude licenses, recording use cases and feeding some into formal innovation processes. Panelists experimented with CoCounsel, VLEX and Clearbrief and subsequently produced a paper and presentations. Engineers also received support to experiment with AI coding. She argues that frontline staff's knowledge of user problems makes AI innovation an organization-wide responsibility rather than an IT-only rollout.
qs: We got them the $20/month GPT licenses, and eventually Claude licenses.
We got them licenses for legal-specific LLM tools—CoCounsel, and eventually VLEX and Clearbrief—so they could do the same: experiment, meet, upload use cases to a shared site.
your IS department, or your IT department, is not your R&D lab with this technology. Your entire staff is your R&D lab.

kp.k: Change management requires incentives, time and technical capacity
kp.d: McCormack identifies job-disruption fears, skepticism and existing workloads as continuing obstacles. AAA credits AI discovery toward innovation KPIs and podcast learning toward training hours, while leadership discusses making room for participation; she explicitly says the time problem remains unresolved. Technical support includes experimentation time, outside consultants, engineer-to-engineer learning and an offshore development bench. Leonard separately frames billable-hour firms as facing short-term revenue losses when allocating time to experimentation.
qs: They have innovation goals, and their KPIs can be satisfied by some of this participation in our generative AI discovery.
I’m not saying we’ve solved it, but we’re always talking about it.
But I think it’s smart for organizations to seriously consider resourcing their IS teams—and their data teams, if they have them.
If they take their foot off the billable hour gas, they’re letting go of revenue in the short term to try to figure this out.

kp.k: AI pilots prioritize learning alongside commercial returns
kp.d: McCormack describes using existing matrices, checklists, design sprints and informal user feedback to prioritize projects, supplemented by a weekly generative-AI steering committee. During the experimental phase, AAA accepts some engineering investments without near-term revenue because learning prepares the organization for larger future bets. She emphasizes resource trade-offs and collective leadership rather than unrestricted pursuit of ideas.
qs: This is still an experimental phase, so we’re willing to do more exploration—build things that cost time from engineers and innovation leaders, but may not bring in revenue—because the learning and training we’re doing is helping prepare for bigger bets down the line.
We now have a separate Gen AI SteerCom—a steering committee that meets once a week to go through our project list and status.

kp.k: ODR acquisition supports a parallel dispute-resolution business
kp.d: McCormack frames acquiring ODR.com and Resourceful Internet Solutions as both improving legacy services and developing a second innovation track, explicitly connecting this approach to Christensen's framework. She predicts demand for faster, cheaper, lighter-touch processes suited to lower-stakes disputes, potentially fully automated, while retaining human hearings for high-stakes matters. Amazon and eBay's longstanding dispute-resolution processes are cited as precedents, not evidence of AAA's new systems' results.
qs: There are lots of disputes that might be better resolved with a lighter touch.
But those same users might also have lower-stakes disputes where a totally different process—a fully online, fast, automated one—makes more sense.
I think we kind of fit the Clayton Christensen model of a successful legacy organization that’s now building a second track for future innovation.

kp.k: AI-enabled dispute resolution could address unmet legal need
kp.d: McCormack argues that generative AI and ODR could serve people and businesses who currently navigate civil disputes alone or abandon them, while enabling creative lawyers to develop new business models. She asserts that 92% of Americans cannot afford help with civil justice problems and extends the affordability concern to small and most medium-sized businesses, without identifying a supporting study. Fast, fair and trustworthy new processes are presented as an aspiration, not demonstrated access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: 92% of Americans can’t afford legal help with their civil justice problems.
I think there will now be tools that provide an operating system for people to resolve disputes—and for lawyers, frankly, to help them.
Especially creative lawyers who want to help with new business models.

kp.k: Clause Builder replaces dropdowns with conversational clause generation
kp.d: McCormack reports that Clause Builder AI became publicly available a few weeks before the episode after beta testing. She describes a GPT-based model trained on AAA's internal clause library, using conversation to elicit requirements and suggest ADR provisions, including for non-lawyer contract users. Internal adversarial and edge-case testing preceded external testing. She acknowledges probabilistic outputs and argues that acceptable clauses need not have identical wording; no quantified reliability or enforceability results are supplied. The tool is described as a service rather than a revenue stream.
qs: So, we trained a GPT-based large language model on that internal data and created a natural language interface.
We trained it internally on that data, then had a lot of internal users practice with it—trying to trick it, giving it difficult or edge-case questions.
And once we got comfortable enough with its outputs (recognizing it’s probabilistic, not deterministic), we made it publicly available.
It’s not a revenue stream for us.

kp.k: Scheduling automation retains arbitrator verification and reduces drafting work
kp.d: McCormack describes an automated scheduling-order generator launched a few months before the episode. It uses a preliminary hearing's Zoom transcript and a tool trained on previous orders to prepare a draft for the arbitrator to review and amend. This is augmentation with human verification, not autonomous adjudication. She states that parties pay less for the task but provides no quantified savings.
qs: After a preliminary hearing in an arbitration, we use the Zoom transcript from that hearing, and a tool trained on a bunch of previous scheduling orders, to produce a draft scheduling order.
They can review and tweak it. And that means the parties pay less for that task.

kp.k: Planned interfaces target filing assistance and neutral selection
kp.d: McCormack identifies a filing chatbot as the next project, particularly for people without lawyers or familiarity with the filing process. A subsequent panelist-search tool would let case managers and eventually users request arbitrator or mediator shortlists in natural language based on dispute subject matter and desired expertise. These are development plans, distinct from the already launched drafting tools.
qs: The next one we’re working on is a filing chatbot—a natural language interface for people filing cases who might not understand the process yet.
We want to give both our case managers (who are trying to put together lists of potential arbitrators or mediators) and eventually users the ability to interact with our data using natural language.

kp.k: Unmanaged employee adoption strengthens the case for AI strategy
kp.d: Leonard reports a May LinkedIn–Microsoft study as showing over 70% of knowledge workers actively using AI and only 60% of organizations actively considering a generative-AI strategy, while noting Microsoft's vested interest. She tentatively recalls 5% having formal training, possibly from another study, and approximately 46% of AI users starting in the preceding six months. No sample or methodology is supplied. Both speakers argue that existing employee use makes organizational guidance urgent; McCormack further anticipates wider use through phone integration.
qs: Microsoft obviously has a vested interest in the Gen AI world—but it shows that over 70% of knowledge workers are actively using AI, whether your organization has an AI strategy or not.
Something like—this might be from a different study—only 5% of organizations have formal training in place to teach workers about generative AI.
I don’t have the exact statistic in front of me—but something like 46% of the people using AI started using it in the last six months.

if you want to make sure they’re using it in ways you think are appropriate, it might make sense to figure out a strategy for your organization—and also think about the cost of not putting a strategy together.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McCormack describes AI already assisting ADR drafting and operations, and predicts expansion into cheaper dispute-resolution processes and previously unmet legal needs. Leonard reports benefits in legal education design and strategic planning.
pts.d: McCormack makes several distinct claims: (1) AAA's publicly launched Clause Builder AI replaces a dropdown-based interaction with a natural-language conversation that offers options and generates an ADR clause suited to the user's needs; probabilistic wording can still produce a good clause. (2) An already launched scheduling-order generator turns a preliminary-hearing Zoom transcript into a draft for an arbitrator to review and adjust, reducing drafting work and what parties pay for that task. (3) A planned filing chatbot will help people understand and navigate case filing, particularly without lawyers; a subsequent panelist-search tool is intended to help case managers and eventually users identify suitable arbitrators or mediators through natural-language queries. (4) AI can shift easily handled portions of staff work to technology, freeing human attention for user-facing value. (5) Combining generative AI with AAA's acquired ODR.com and Resourceful Internet Solutions capabilities can support new, faster and cheaper dispute-resolution options, including fully online automated processes for lower-stakes disputes alongside human-led high-stakes proceedings. She predicts increasing demand for such options, not wholesale replacement of arbitration or mediation. (6) These tools could reach people and businesses previously unable to obtain legal help, while enabling creative lawyers to serve them through new business models. Leonard separately reports that Claude helped her and her partner develop workshop activities for lawyers, saving time and benefiting clients, and that LLM use offered useful strategic business-planning suggestions. Both speakers describe hallucinations and unpredictable outputs as barriers to legal adoption, while arguing that existing employee use makes organizational AI strategies urgent.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source primarily offers implementation accounts and personal experience, supplemented by an adoption survey and historical ODR examples; it does not provide quantified outcome evaluations of AAA's tools.
pts.d: McCormack's product claims draw on her firsthand account as AAA president and CEO. She says Clause Builder AI was trained on AAA's internal clause library and subjected to internal edge-case testing and external user testing before launch. The scheduling tool reportedly uses previous scheduling orders and hearing transcripts. Neither account supplies measured accuracy, time savings, fee reductions, enforceability outcomes, or comparative benchmarks. AAA's reported scale—over half a million cases in the preceding year, about 720 staff and over 5,000 independent panelists—provides organizational context rather than evidence of AI effectiveness. Staff and panelist experimentation, use-case sharing, and panelists' papers and presentations supply experiential support for potential workflow benefits. Jason Cabrera's task matrix is described as models' assessments of their own ability to handle job tasks, not a measured finding that they performed those tasks successfully. Leonard's workshop and strategy examples are personal anecdotes. McCormack invokes longstanding Amazon and eBay ODR use as precedent for lighter-touch dispute resolution, not as a test of generative AI. Her access-to-justice prediction is motivated by an uncited statement that 92% of Americans cannot afford help with civil justice problems and by her account of business unmet need; no demonstrated access gains are reported. Leonard cites a May LinkedIn–Microsoft study for over 70% knowledge-worker AI use and approximately 60% of organizations considering a strategy, while noting Microsoft's commercial interest. She is uncertain whether the approximately 5% formal-training figure comes from another study and qualifies the approximately 46% recent-adopter figure as recalled rather than exact. These are cross-domain adoption figures, not legal-sector measurements. The speakers cite the New York lawyer's fabricated-case filing and McCormack's experience presenting to Missouri appellate judges as evidence of hallucination-related resistance, without reporting a model hallucination rate.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2024 conversation distinguishes tools already launched from a near-term development pipeline and an undated broader transformation; benefits depend on suitable use cases, human expertise, testing and organizational support.
pts.d: McCormack dates her expectation of significant, probably rapid legal-sector change to the interval between ChatGPT's November 2022 release and her February 2023 arrival at AAA. At the time of the episode, Clause Builder AI had gone live a few weeks earlier after beta testing; the scheduling-order generator had launched a few months earlier. The filing chatbot is described as next in development, followed provisionally by panelist search, without delivery dates. Expansion into underserved markets and new dispute-resolution models is prospective and has no firm deadline; the podcast's '2030 Vision' title does not establish a 2030 deadline for these claims. McCormack qualifies deployment by the probabilistic nature of outputs and describes releasing Clause Builder once testers were comfortable enough with them, not after establishing perfect reliability. Scheduling-order use explicitly retains human verification through arbitrator review and adjustment. Leonard conditions useful creative assistance on domain expertise to reject unsuitable suggestions and adapt promising ones. Automated dispute resolution is presented as appropriate for some lower-stakes matters, while high-stakes clients may continue to require human testimony assessment. Organizational benefits require participation beyond IT, time to experiment, training, leadership engagement and technical capacity. McCormack describes the current phase as experimental and accepts projects without immediate revenue for their learning value. The speakers argue for strategies now because workers already use AI; McCormack also anticipates wider use as AI reaches phones, but gives no precise rollout date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern ADR parties, self-represented people and businesses, arbitrators and mediators, AAA staff, lawyers developing new services, and legal organizations managing employee adoption.
pts.d: For individuals and businesses drafting contracts, including nonlawyers, Clause Builder offers conversational assistance with ADR clauses as a service rather than an AAA revenue stream. For arbitration parties, scheduling automation is claimed to lower charges for a specific drafting task; arbitrators remain responsible for reviewing and adjusting the draft. Self-represented filers are the especially emphasized beneficiaries of the planned filing chatbot. Case managers and eventually clients would use natural-language panelist search to assemble candidate lists. Existing large-business clients could choose different processes for different stakes rather than abandoning human-led ADR altogether. Separately, people and smaller organizations with unmet civil legal needs are the intended access-to-justice beneficiaries of future faster, trustworthy processes; McCormack also explicitly includes medium-sized businesses in her account of unmet need. Lawyers willing to adopt new business models could serve these previously unserved markets. AAA marketing staff, HR, case managers, engineers and independent panelists are portrayed as participants in developing and benefiting from new workflows, not merely recipients of an IT rollout. Job disruption is acknowledged as a source of fear, but the transcript does not predict a headcount reduction or quantify lawyer displacement. Leonard identifies a particular adoption constraint for hourly billing law firms: time diverted to experimentation can sacrifice short-term revenue. Organizational leaders and judicial managers face the need to guide existing employee use rather than assume non-adoption. Leonard's own legal-education clients reportedly benefit from AI-assisted workshop design.
